title: Selective Reduction of CO2 to CO on an Sb-Modified Cu Electrode: Spontaneous Fabrication and Physical Insight
abstract: Electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) on Cu is often plagued by low selectivity and stability because of less-controlled preparation of electrocatalytic materials as well as insufficient understanding of the structure−performance relation. In this work, we develop a facile galvanic displacement protocol, involving an electropolished Cu sheet in a mixed Sb(III)−Cl− precursor solution, to form an Sb-modified Cu electrode that can selectively convert CO2 to CO with a Faradaic efficiency of ca. 82% and an undecayed reduction current over 12 h. Moreover, in situ infrared spectroscopy detects a relatively weak and red-shifted CO band on the Sb-modified Cu electrode as compared to that on the Cu electrode at potentials of CO2RR. Density functional theory calculations reveal that the Sb clusters on the Cu surface change the electronic structures of Cu as well as Sb and thus weaken the CO binding strength on Cu sites, consistent with the observed CO band feature and high CO selectivity. These findings may shed light on the rational design of high-selectivity CO2RR electrocatalysts by proper interfacial structure engineering.

sections.text: KEYWORDS: carbon dioxide reduction reaction, antimony-modified copper, carbon monoxide selectivity, IR spectroscopy, density functional theory calculations, galvanic displacement

sections.heading: 1. INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
Electrochemical carbon dioxide reduction reaction (CO2RR) is a promising process to reduce the excess CO2 levels in the atmosphere and at the same time convert CO2 into valuable chemicals.1,2 More importantly, this reaction can be conducted at ambient conditions with renewable electricity inputs such as solar power, wind power, and hydropower.3 It is known that the CO2RR products such as CO, hydrocarbons, and oxygenates depend largely on the chemical nature of metal electrodes.4−6 In the study of electrocatalysis of CO2RR, two key aspects are to tune up the selectivity of a specific product through certain structural control of a catalyst and provide a physical insight into the performance of the resulting catalyst.6−9
Cu is the unique metal capable of reducing CO2 into various products including the C1 and C2 compounds.5,10,11 Nevertheless, the selectivity for a specific product of CO2RR is not high on the monometallic Cu electrode. Several strategies have been reported so far to regulate a specific product selectivity for CO2RR on Cu-based catalysts, including but not limited to admolecule or adatom modification,12−20 restructuring surface layers,21−27 and alloying (doping) with another element.28−30 Among these tuning knobs, construction of bimetallic catalysts by surface engineering on Cu substrates has attracted considerable interest. For instance, it was found that the Cu substrate either underpotentially deposited with Pb adatoms or electrodeposited with Bi clusters could selectively convert CO2
to formate over a large potential window.14,24,26 An enhanced CO2-to-hydrocarbon conversion was reported on a Cu foil modified with an atomically deposited Pd layer.15,19 An increased selectivity toward ethylene production was attained on tiny Ag nanoparticle-anchored larger Cu nanocores28 and electrodeposited Cu/Sn alloy electrode.29
Notably, despite the fact that Cu, Ag, and Au are in the same IB group, Cu is markedly different from Ag and Au in terms of CO2RR product distribution, given that the latter two produce CO predominantly.31 To target highly selective CO production on Cu-based electrodes, Cu and In (or Sn) composite oxide-derived catalysts were reported in favor of CO formation.16−18 Sb deserves special attention, given its peculiar local environment-dependent behavior in CO2RR. Among others, a bulk Sb electrode and an Sb-modified Pt (or Pb) electrode produce overwhelmingly H2 while single-Sb atoms dispersed on different carbon substrates yield either CO or formate.32−34 While reduced CuO−Sb2O3 nanocomposites (via coprecipitation reaction in the solvent ethanol)35 and Cu2Sb-decorated Cu nanowire arrays (via electrodeposition

followed by annealing)36 could selectively convert CO2 into CO, SbOx@CuyO synthesized by precipitation and calcination favored the CO2-to-formate conversion.
37 These rather conflicting reports suggest that the product selectivity of CO2RR on Sb-containing catalysts may be tailored by different fabrication methods. In this context, it is demanded to explore a facile and reproducible fabrication of an Sb-modified Cu electrode that enables the selective CO2-to-CO conversion and understand the structure−performance relation. The latter calls for the molecular-level in situ spectroscopy38,39 to provide the dynamic interfacial chemistry as well as the modeling calculations40−44 to disclose the energetic aspect along the reaction coordinate. Unfortunately, no such a combined study of CO2RR to CO on the Sb−Cu catalytic electrode has been reported so far. In this work, a facile spontaneous galvanic displacement approach is developed to prepare an Sb nanocluster-decorated Cu (Sb−Cu) electrode in a chloride-rich acidic solution, yielding a much higher CO selectivity for CO2RR than that on a pristine Cu electrode. In situ attenuated total reflection surface-enhanced infrared absorption spectroscopy (ATRSEIRAS) measurements and density function theory (DFT) calculations are combined to provide a physical insight into the high CO2 to CO conversion selectivity on the Sb-modified Cu electrode, revealing a weakened CO adsorption on electronic structure-modified Cu sites.

sections.heading: 2. EXPERIMENTAL AND COMPUTATIONAL METHODS
sections.text:
2.1. Chemicals and Materials. A Cu foil (99.99%, 20 mm × 20 mm × 0.2 mm) was purchased from ZNXC Company, SbCl3 (99.99%, trace-metal basis) and KHCO3 (99.99%, tracemetal basis) were purchased from Aladdin Company, and highpurity CO2 (99.999%) and Ar (99.999%) were from Air Liquid Company. All chemicals were used without further purification. 2.2. Preparation of Catalytic Electrodes. To prepare the Sb−Cu bimetallic catalytic electrode, the Cu foil was electropolished according to the procedures described previously.23 The electropolished Cu foil was then placed in the solution containing 0.5 mM SbCl3, 0.5 M HCl, and 0.2 M KCl at 25 °C for a desired period of time, leading to the formation of a pale-purple bimetallic appearance on the electropolished Cu foil. During the above immersion, a spontaneous galvanic displacement process took place. Control experiment was also conducted in the absence of Cl− or Sb(III) in the soaking solution. The formation of surface layers via the galvanic displacement process will be discussed later. To prepare the neat Sb catalytic electrode, 20 mg of Sb nanoparticles (synthesized according to a published work37), 500 μL of isopropanol, 500 μL of water, and 60 μL of Nafion were mixed and sonicated to form a catalyst ink, followed by being sprayed on a carbon paper with the Sb mass loading 1.6 mg cm−2. 2.3. Material Characterization. Surface morphologies of the electropolished Cu foils before and after the above galvanic displacement were imaged by atomic force microscopy (AFM, Cypher, Oxford Instruments) with a tapping mode. High-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF−STEM) and high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) were performed on a Tecnai G2 F20 STwin (FEI Company, USA) at an accelerating voltage of 200 kV. To identify the crystalline phases of surface films, grazing-
incidence X-ray diffraction (GIXRD) patterns of Sb-modified Cu electrodes from 20 to 80° were recorded with a Rigaku SmartLab X-ray diffractometer using the Cu Kα radiation incidence (40 kV, 30 mA) at a grazing angle of 0.5°. The surface electronic structures of the overfilm were analyzed by using an ESCALAB 250 XI X-ray photoelectron spectrometer (Thermo Scientific) with the monochromatic Al Kα radiation (1486.6 eV), and the binding energies were calibrated with reference to the C 1s peak at 284.6 eV.
2.4. CO2RR Measurements and Quantification of Products. All CO2 electroreduction measurements were carried out at room temperature in a customized H-type cell as described in our previous report.45 An Sb-modified Cu electrode served as the working electrode with a graphite rod and a Ag/AgCl electrode used as the counter electrode and the reference electrode, respectively. A CHI 660b electrochemical workstation (CH Instruments, Shanghai) was employed for the potential control and current measurement. Unless otherwise specified, all potentials reported in this work were converted to the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) scale, with a manual iR drop compensation at 70% level. Before CO2RR measurements, the electrode was pretreated at −0.6 V versus RHE for 15 min in an Ar-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 toward a stable surface state. The gas products were analyzed by an online gas chromatography (GC, 2060 Ramiin Instruments) equipped with a thermal conductivity detector and a flame ionization detector coupled with a methanizer. The aqueous products were analyzed by a 500 MHz 1H nuclear magnetic resonance spectrometer (NMR, Bruker Company) with a water suppression technique using DMSO as the internal standard.
2.5. In Situ ATR-SEIRAS Measurements. The Cu, Sb, and Sb-modified Cu films on Au-coated Si prism were used as the working electrodes for in situ ATR-SEIRAS measurement, with the Ag/AgCl electrode and the graphite rod as the reference and counter electrodes, respectively. The details of the ATR-SEIRAS setup and experimental methods were also described previously.45,46 Potentiodynamic ATR-SEIRAS measurement was conducted in CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3. Prior to and during the ATR-SEIRAS measurement, ∼10 sccm CO2 flow was kept bubbling through the spectroelectrochemical cell to agitate the electrolyte to facilitate the saturation and transport of dissolved CO2.
2.6. DFT Calculations. All the DFT calculations were performed by using the Vienna Ab Initio Simulation Package47 with the Perdew−Burke−Ernzerhof (PBE) functional in the generalized gradient approximation,48,49 and the DFT-D3 method with Becke−Johnson damping was employed to correct the van der Waals interactions of the reaction system. A cutoff energy of 450 eV was used, the Methfessel−Paxton method with a broadening factor was 0.1 eV, and the convergence criteria of energy and force were set to 10−6 eV and 0.01 eV/Å, respectively. The Γ-centered k-point sampling grid of 12 × 12 × 12 was adopted for the primitive cell calculation. The calculated lattice constant of Cu was 3.568 Å. A six-layer (2 × 2) supercell with the bottom two layers fixed was used to optimize of the modeled Cu structure, and the vacuum spacing is 15 Å. The Γ-centered k-point sampling grid adopted 6 × 6 × 1 and 48 × 48 × 1 for the geometric optimization and the projected density of states (PDOS) plot. To build the model for Sb atoms on Cu, the adsorption energy of Sb atoms on the Cu(111) surface was calculated. For an Sb primitive cell, the Sb−Sb bond length is about 4.32 Å. In
https://doi.org/10.1021/acscatal.1c00860 ACS Catal. 2021, 11, 6846−6856

contrast, the Cu−Cu bond length is about 2.53 Å. As a result, it is not possible for all Sb atoms to adsorb on most stable sites of Cu(111), and the most favorable model should be two layers of Sb atom covering on a three-layer Cu(111) (6 × 2) supercell with the bottom layer of Sb atoms occupying the bridge and fcc sites of the Cu(111) surface, leading to an Sb surface tension of 5.87%. The Γ-centered k-point sampling grid adopted 1 × 2 × 1 and 10 × 20 × 1 for the geometric optimization and the PDOS plot. The vibrational frequencies of adsorbed molecules were calculated with the finite difference method assuming that all metal atoms were frozen. In addition, the external electrostatic field and dipole correction were used in the frequency calculation to simulate the Stark effect.50

sections.heading: 3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
sections.text:
3.1. Formation of the Sb−Cu Electrode by Galvanic Displacement. An Sb-modified Cu (or simply Sb−Cu) electrode was obtained by immersing an electropolished Cu sheet in a solution containing 0.5 mM SbCl3, 0.5 M HCl, and 0.2 M KCl where the galvanic displacement reaction between Cu and Sb(III) species may occur as shown in Figure 1. Cu+ ions are easily coordinated with Cl− to form [CuClx] 1−x (x =
1−3) complexes,53 and Sb3+ ions coordinated with chloride to form [SbClx]
3−x (x = 1−6) complexes,54 depending on the total chloride ion concentration in acidic media. As a result, the anodic oxidation of Cu may proceed at relatively negative potentials to reduce the coordinated Sb(III) ions in concentrated HCl media.55 The standard equilibrium potential for Cu+ + e− = Cu, Eθ(Cu+/Cu) = 0.521 V versus SHE,56 and that for Sb3+ + 3e− = Sb, Eθ(Sb3+/Sb) = 0.24 V versus SHE.57 At a first glance, Sb3+ may not be reduced to Sb by the anodic oxidation of Cu to Cu+. However, in the presence of a sufficiently high concentration of Cl−, CuCl3 2− and SbCl6
3− are the dominant species. Eθ(CuCl3
2−/Cu) is shifted to 0.125 V at 25 °C by taking the complexing constant into account53 while Eθ(SbCl6
3−/Sb) is shifted to 0.159 V.54 Alternatively, the Cu dissolution reaction may proceed according to
+ → ↓ + =θ− − ECu Cl CuCl e 0.121 V vs SHE (4)
with Eθ calculated based on Ksp of CuCl. 56 Thus, the galvanic displacement reaction between the coordinated Sb(III) species and Cu may occur spontaneously. Also noted is that the actual concentration of Cl− is far greater than the total concentration of various forms of Sb(III) or Cu(I) species. According to a previous report,55 as the gross molar ratio of Cl/Sb is higher than 15, the concentration of free Sb3+ is lower than about 2.3 × 10−7 mol L−1, and given 2.5 × 10−13 mol L−1 for the initial free Cu+ ions, the equilibrium reduction potentials for the following two redox couples are calculated to be

Therefore, this potential difference further suggests that the reduction of SbCl6 3− to Sb at the expense of Cu to CuCl3 2− is thermodynamically viable at room temperature. It should be mentioned here that the complexing effect of chloride ions plays a key role in enabling the above galvanic displacement reaction. In fact, such a reaction does not occur in an Sb(III)containing sulfuric acid or perchloric acid solution in the absence of chloride ions.55
3.2. Characterizations of the As-Prepared Cu and Sb−Cu Electrodes. The AFM images in Figure 2a,b reveal
https://doi.org/10.1021/acscatal.1c00860 ACS Catal. 2021, 11, 6846−6856
6848
that the morphology of the Cu surface changes after Sb modification. A relatively smooth Cu surface could be observed after electropolishing despite the presence of grain boundaries while the cuboid-like nanoparticles were homogeneously packed on the Cu substrate after the immersion in the Sb(III) and Cl−-containing electrolyte (also see Figure S1). The average surface roughness factor (Sa) increases from 2.2 nm for Cu to 5.8 nm for Sb-modified Cu as derived from Figure 2. To further quantify the surface roughness of Cu and Sb-modified Cu electrodes, the double-layer capacitances were measured, showing that the relative surface roughness of the Sb−Cu to Cu electrode was ca. 1.43 (Figure S2). Figure 2c shows the HAADF−STEM image and the corresponding EDX mapping of a typical cuboid-like nanoparticle acquired by scratching and sonicating the as-formed Sb−Cu electrode in ethanol, indicative of the Cu, Sb, Cl, and O components (Figure S3). The nanoparticle shows a core@ shell-like structure with the Cu core and the mixed shell of Cu/ Sb, which is further reinforced by the EDX line scan elemental profiles in Figure 2d. The HRTEM image shows numerous lattice fringes with d spacings of 0.19, 0.24, and 0.21 nm measured by two neighboring crystal lattice planes corresponding to the (220), (111), and (511) interplanar spacings of CuCl, Cu2O, and Sb2O3 phases, as a result of the exposure in the ambient atmosphere during the post-treatment and transfer of the as-synthesized sample. Note that the lattice fringe of 0.18 nm corresponds to that of Cu(200) (Figure S4). To probe the near-surface chemical states of the Sb−Cu electrode, core-level X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) measurement was carried out for the Sb−Cu electrode. In the survey spectrum (Figure S5), only C (the common impurity),
O, Cl, Cu, and Sb elements were observed in good agreement with the above EDS mapping results. For the Cu 2p region, the two major peaks at 932.4 and 952.2 eV in Figure 3a correspond to the 2p3/2 and 2p5/2 doublet peaks of Cu(0) or Cu(I) species, respectively.23 The presence of Cu(I) can also be deduced from the peak at 915.7 eV of Cu KII (Figure S5), while the two satellite peaks at ∼935 and ∼944 eV of the above two doublets are due to Cu(II) species. Furthermore, the Sb-modified Cu electrode displays the Sb 3d doublet peaks (Figure 3a). The two doublet peaks at 530.5 and 539.7 eV correspond to Sb2O3, and the two at 528.2 and 537.6 eV correspond to metallic Sb. The spectral deconvolution for the Sb 3d region leads to an Sb(III) to Sb(0) ratio of ∼9:1, arising possibly from the sample exposure in the ambient air. For the Cl 2p region, the two peaks at 198.7 and 200.3 eV are ascribed to Cl 2p3/2 and 2p1/2 of CuCl (see Figure S5), 58 respectively, consistent with the anodic oxidation of eq 4, as well as the lattice fringe analysis from HRTEM imaging (Figure S4). Further componential analysis on other Sb−Cu control samples with different immersion times is summarized in Table S1. To better probe the near-surface crystalline structure of the
as-prepared electrodes, GIXRD measurements were comparatively conducted for the Cu (Figure S6) and Sb−Cu (Figure 3b) electrodes at a grazing angle of 0.5°. For Sb−Cu, the 2θ diffraction peaks at 26.65, 34.95, 54.73, 82.87, and 87.0° are indexed to Sb2O3 (JCPDS 72-1854). The 36.09 and 74.37° peaks are indexed to Cu2O (JCPDS 34-1354) and the 53.1 and 65.37° ones to CuCl (JCPDS 30-0472). The peaks for Sb (66.03°, JCPDS 85-1322) and Cu (43.46, 50.62, and 74.40°,
https://doi.org/10.1021/acscatal.1c00860 ACS Catal. 2021, 11, 6846−6856
6849
JCPDS 85-1326) are also observed. Noteworthy, no Cu−Sb alloy phases can be identified from the GIXRD result. Prior to the CO2RR measurement, the Sb−Cu electrode was subjected to a pre-reduction at −0.6 V in Ar-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 for 15 min to attain a stable cathodic current, and the
ex situ AFM image of the reduced Sb−Cu electrode shown in Figure S7 shows a morphological change from cuboid to cauliflower-like nanoparticles. The ex situ EDX mapping (Figure S8) and XPS survey (Figure S9) spectra of this Sb− Cu sample suggest the presence of Cu and Sb elements but the absence of Cl element, although the surface oxides are detectable due to the sample transfer in the ambient air. In Figure S10, the GIXRD pattern of reduced Sb−Cu also indicates the absence of the CuCl diffraction peak at 65.37°, which is probably arisen from the CuCl reduction to Cu.58 The pre-reduction treatment rules out the halide effect on the CO2RR product distribution. 59,60
The combined ex situ HRTEM, EDS elemental mapping, XPS, and GIXRD characterizations indicate that the surface film of the as-prepared Sb−Cu electrode is composed of individual nanoscale phases of CuCl, Sb, Cu, and their oxides after its exposure in the ambient air. In other words, Sb and Cu nanocomposites are likely to form in the surface film of the Sb−Cu electrode being subjected to the CO2RR practice. In consideration of the underlying Cu, the thus-obtained Sb−Cu electrode may be envisioned as one Cu electrode homogeneously decorated with Sb adclusters in DFT calculations.
3.3. Electrochemical CO2RR Performance. Figure S11 shows the negatively going linear sweep voltammograms recorded at 50 mV s−1 for the Cu and Sb−Cu electrodes in either Ar-saturated or CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3. In the Arsaturated electrolyte, a much lower current density is seen on the Sb−Cu electrode together with a higher onset potential compared to the counterpart on the Cu electrode, indicative of a largely suppressed HER performance on the Sb−Cu electrode. In the CO2-saturated electrolyte, the CO2RR onset potentials are close on both the Sb−Cu and Cu electrodes. Notably, the cathodic current is enhanced by a larger factor on the Sb−Cu electrode than on the Cu electrode when the Ar-
https://doi.org/10.1021/acscatal.1c00860 ACS Catal. 2021, 11, 6846−6856
6850
saturated electrolyte is replaced by the CO2-saturated one, suggestive of a more facile CO2RR kinetics on the Sb−Cu electrode. Figure 4a,b shows the FEs of CO, formate, and H2 for CO2RR on Sb−Cu and Cu electrodes in CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 at varied potentials. The FEs of other products are shown in Figure S12. The Sb−Cu electrode shows a much higher selectivity toward CO and a lower selectivity toward the H2 side product. For instance, the FE of CO reaches up to ∼82% at ∼−1.1 V on Sb−Cu, while the highest FE of CO is ca. 16% at −0.96 V and decreases to 2.5% at ∼−1.1 V on Cu, which is in good agreement with a previous report on an electropolished Cu.61 In fact, the CO production selectivity on the Sb−Cu electrode is comparable to that on the Ag electrode (Figure S13). Formate is a minor CO2RR product with its FE being 8.0− 12.0% on the Sb−Cu electrode, while the FE of formate decreases from 24.3 to 2.8% on Cu in the same potential range from −0.87 to −1.18 V. Besides, the FE of H2 on Cu exceeds that on the Sb−Cu electrode over the potential window under investigation. Figure 4c depicts the total current density and CO partial current density on Cu and Sb−Cu electrodes. At a small overpotential region, jtotal on the Sb−Cu electrode is slightly larger than that on Cu, probably arisen from the larger electrochemical surface area of the former (Figure S2). While at overpotentials more negative than −1.1 V, Cu delivers a larger jtotal due to the generation of >2e
− reduction products. A dramatic difference is observed for the CO partial current density on the two electrodes, that is, more than 100 times higher jCO is noted on the Sb−Cu electrode as compared to pure Cu at −1.18 V. Figure 4d shows the long-term stability of the Sb−Cu electrode-catalyzed CO evolution at −1.1 V, which maintains ∼80% CO selectivity during the 12 h continuous electrolysis. Furthermore, the XPS (Figure S14) and GIXRD (Figure S15) characterizations of the Sb−Cu electrode after the extended CO2RR operation demonstrate a satisfactory structural stability. The immersion time for the electropolished Cu in an Sb(III) and Cl−-containing bath may affect the surface Sb/Cu atomic ratio and thus the product distribution in CO2RR. Table S1 shows the variation of such an atomic ratio as a function of immersion time. For the immersion time 100 s, the surface Sb/Cu atomic ratio is around 1:4.62, leading to a CO FE of ca. 50% at −1.1 V. It can be seen that when the
immersion time is longer than 300 s, the Sb/Cu atomic ratio tends to stabilize at ∼1:3.3, with a steady CO selectivity around 80% noted for CO2RR on the resulting Sb−Cu electrodes, virtually regardless of the immersion time (Figure S12). To emphasize the role of Sb(III) and Cl− ions in the
Sb(III)/Cu displacement reaction, two more control experiments were carried out at the absence of either Sb(III) or Cl−
ions in the immersion solution. The resulting Cu electrodes yielded virtually no change of CO2RR product distribution as compared to an electropolished Cu electrode (Figures S16 and S17), suggesting that Sb(III) and Cl− ions in the immersion solution are essential to obtain the Sb−Cu electrode that enables a selective CO production in CO2RR. As discussed above, the Sb−Cu electrode via the galvanic displacement consists of more likely Sb and Cu nanocomposites rather than Sb and Cu bimetallic alloys covered on the Cu substrate. Notably, in a previous report, the carbon paper-supported CuxSby alloy catalyst produces less than 10% CO FE in CO2RR at potentials negative of −0.99 V,62 in support of our proposition. In fact, we also applied a potential pulse of −0.4 V (vs SCE) for 20 s to an electropolished Cu sheet in a plating bath of 0.5 mM potassium antimony tartrate, 0.2 M K2SO4 and 0.11 M H2SO4, to obtain an Sb-deposited Cu electrode which, without any optimization, is able to yield a CO FE higher than 70% for CO2RR in the otherwise same conditions (Figure S18) approaching to that on the galvanic displacement-based Sb−Cu electrode. All the above observations argue against the significant formation of the surface bimetallic alloy in the Sb− Cu electrode fabricated by spontaneous galvanic displacement.
3.4. In Situ Electrochemical ATR-SEIRAS. Molecularlevel understanding of markedly different CO selectivities for CO2RR on the Cu and Sb−Cu electrodes was assisted by highsensitivity electrochemical ATR-SEIRAS. The control measurement of CO2RR on a pristine Sb film was also performed, without appreciable CO species being observed during the same potential sweep (Figure S19), which is in agreement with the bulk electrolysis result as shown in Figure S20. Figure 5 shows the in situ ATR-SEIRA spectra acquired for the Cu and Sb−Cu electrodes in CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 during a negative-going potential sweep from 0.1 to −1.1 V (Figure 5a).

6851
The integrated intensity and the frequency of the COL band as a function of applied potential are depicted in Figure 5b. On both electrodes, the onset potentials for discerning the COL bands are around −0.4 V, and the COL band intensities are weaker on Sb−Cu than on Cu. Furthermore, Figure 5b shows a bell-shaped band intensity versus potential profile on Cu with the maximum at ca. −0.8 V compared to an increasing band intensity versus potential profile on Sb−Cu from −0.5 to −1.1 V. The relatively weaker COL band on the Sb−Cu electrode and the higher CO selectivity during CO2RR indicate a more facile desorption of the CO intermediate from the Sb− Cu surface to form gaseous CO. In fact, according to our DFT calculations in the next section, the intermediate CO adsorption is thermodynamically more favorable and the subsequent CO desorption is less favorable on Cu than on Sb− Cu (Figure 6, vide inf ra). On the Cu electrode, the COL band
intensity starts to decrease at potentials negative of −0.8 V accompanied by the evolution of CH4 and C2H4, demonstrating that the surface CO species serves as the precursor for their production63 rather than directly desorbs to form gaseous CO. Overall, the COL peaks are red-shifted and broadened on the Sb−Cu electrode, in comparison to the counterparts on Cu at given potentials, as can be seen from Figure 5b as well as from the simulated calculation result in Figure S21. The broader COL band may indicate multiple kinds of Cu sites to accommodate COL adsorption. For instance, COL adsorption on Cu terrace and defect sites may yield the bands at ∼2040 and 2080 cm−1, respectively.64 The above observation suggests that Sb adclusters may preferentially occupy the defective Cu
sites. For a given electrode, the COL band frequencies increase initially and then decrease with a negatively going potential, given the combined Stark effect and the dipole−dipole coupling effect. The former causes the COL band frequency shifted to a lower wavenumber with decreasing potential (the simulated Stark effect for CO on both surfaces can be seen in Figure S21), while the latter is related to the COL coverage, the higher the COL coverage, the higher wavenumber on the same electrode. The generally lower frequency of the COL band on Sb−Cu than on Cu may be attributed to the much lower CO coverage on the Sb−Cu electrode during CO2RR at a given potential. In fact, in a CO-dosing control experiment, the COL bands for saturated CO adsorption on Sb−Cu appear much weaker and broader at lower frequencies as compared to the counterparts on Cu (see Figure S22). Alternatively, the lower COL band frequencies on Sb−Cu may be understood by the DFT calculation in terms of a larger bond length of CO and a bent ∠Cu−C−O of the adsorbed CO on the Sb-modified Cu(111) surface (Figure 7, vide infra). As will be discussed next, CO adsorption and desorption occur on Cu sites rather than on Sb sites of the Sb-modified Cu surface.
3.5. DFT Calculations. To elucidate the enhanced CO selectivity on the Sb−Cu electrode, the relative stability of reaction intermediates was theoretically estimated for the CO pathways of CO2RR on the Cu surface with and without Sb modification. The optimized configuration for Sb deposition on Cu(111) obtained by DFT calculations reveals that Sb adatoms are most stable to locate at the bridge or fcc sites on Cu(111) (Figure S23). The simulated Sb−Cu surface is referred to Sb−Cu(111). Figure S24 plots the PDOS for the dbands of surface Cu atoms, for which the d-band center is located at −2.24 eV for Cu(111) and −2.35 eV for Sb− Cu(111). The downshifted d-band center for the latter is generally recognized in favor of weakening CO adsorption on the Sb−Cu(111), and the adsorption energy of *CO on the Sb−Cu(111) surface (−0.24 eV) is much smaller than that of Cu(111) (−0.88 eV) and closer to that on Au(111) and Ag(111) (ca. −0.40 and −0.32 eV, respectively, see Table S2). Thus, the desorption of the *CO species is much more facile on the Sb−Cu(111) surface. In other words, the stronger CO binding on Cu than on Ag or Au may at least partly account for the lower CO2 to CO selectivity on a bare Cu electrode. Thus,
https://doi.org/10.1021/acscatal.1c00860 ACS Catal. 2021, 11, 6846−6856
6852
a guideline for developing a Cu-based electrocatalyst with a high CO2 to CO selectivity is to tune down the CO adsorption strength on Cu sites by means of surface modification or alloying. In this work, neither *CO nor CO(g) species on the Sb electrode was observed by in situ ATR-SEIRAS and online GC; in contrast, both *CO and CO(g) were detected on bare Cu and Sb-modified Cu electrodes. The highly dispersed Sb adclusters on the Cu surface may not only modify the electronic structure of the neighboring Cu sites but also segregate the CO adsorption on Cu sites geometrically, leading to a weakened CO adsorption strength, in favor of CO desorption. In fact, the weaker and broader CO bands at ca. 2020−2060 cm−1 are attributable to the linearly adsorbed CO on exposed Cu sites of the Sb-modified Cu electrode. Therefore, the exposed Cu sites around or close to the Sb atoms are likely the main active sites for efficient CO2-to-CO conversion. This deduction is further reinforced by theoretical simulation data (see Table S3), showing that the *COOH adsorption on Cu sites is stronger than that on Sb sites at the Cu/Sb interface. Similarly, the preferential *CO adsorption on Cu sites was also suggested for CO2RR on the Cu3Sn alloy 44 and the Cu−Ag and Cu−Sn alloys.29 Figure 6a depicts the charge density difference of Sb− Cu(111) surface upon CO2 adsorption, where a slight charge transfer from Sb to Cu (ca. 0.1 e−) can be found by Bader charge analysis and the adsorption of reaction intermediates is more likely on Cu sites than on Sb sites (Table S2). Thus, in this work, we only consider the adsorption of relevant species on Cu sites. Figure 6b plots the free energy variation against the reaction coordinate for the CO2-to-CO conversion on Cu(111) and Sb−Cu(111) surfaces at 0 and −0.5 V versus CHE. As can be seen from the calculation results, at either potential, the formation of *CO on Cu(111) is energetically more favorable than on Sb−Cu(111), given a much smaller reaction energy to cross for the former. The weaker *CO adsorption on Sb−Cu(111) is consistent with the calculated lower d-band center. Lowering the potential from 0 to −0.5 V (vs CHE), decreasing the reaction energy on both surfaces, facilitates the *CO formation on both surfaces. No matter which potential is applied, the *CO adsorption strength on Sb−Cu(111) is much weaker than that on Cu(111), benefiting the *CO desorption to form free CO. In addition, the higher reaction energy from the state of CO2 + 2H
+ + 2e− to the state of *CO + H2O may suggest that a more negative potential is needed to initialize *CO on Sb−Cu(111), which is qualitatively consistent with infrared spectral result, see Figure 5b. For CO adsorption on Cu sites with or without Sb modification, the change of orbital interaction between Cu and CO may interpret the adsorption energy and the ν(CO) vibration frequency shift. Figure 7 shows the peak shapes of the PDOS. Compared with a free CO molecule, the σ energy level of adsorbed CO shifts down by −7.5 eV. Meanwhile, a new PDOS peak of Cu is formed upon CO adsorption due to the σ−d interaction. It is noted that the energy level of σ orbital of the adsorbed CO on Cu(111) is lower than that on Sb− Cu(111), leading to a stronger σ−d interaction and thus a shorter bond length of Cu−C on Cu(111) (ca. 1.84 Å) than that on Sb−Cu(111) (ca. 1.87 Å). On the other hand, the modified Sb also influences the adsorbed CO. As shown in Figure S25, the orbital overlap between s, p electrons of Sb, and π* orbital of *CO can be observed, and a weak interaction
between Sb and CO is also found in the occupied orbital region, leading to an increased C−O bond length (i.e., 1.16 Å) and a bent ∠Cu−C−O (i.e.,178°). Note that the C−O bond length for CO adsorbed on Cu(111) is 1.15 Å, and the corresponding ∠Cu−C−O is 180°.65 The larger bond length of CO and bent ∠Cu−C−O of the adsorbed CO on Sb− Cu(111) suggest that the bond energy of C−O on Sb− Cu(111) is smaller than that on Cu(111). In other words, a higher vibration frequency of CO is expected on Cu(111) than that on Sb−Cu(111), which is in good agreement with the above infrared spectral result. Notably, the above DFT calculation results are qualitatively consistent with the experimental observations, although we have not taken into consideration explicitly the effect of charged electric double layer on the CO2RR kinetics. A recent work presents a new multi-scale modeling scheme that integrates ab initio reaction kinetics with mass transport simulations,66 enabling to explain overpotential-dependent rate-determining steps for CO2RR on Au electrodes. Such a methodology is expected to provide more details of the CO2RR mechanism on Cu-based electrodes.

sections.heading: 4. CONCLUSIONS
sections.text:
We have investigated the electrocatalytic CO2RR on Sbmodified Cu electrodes prepared by a galvanic displacement protocol involving the immersion of an electropolished Cu in an Sb(III)-precursor acidic solution containing excessive amount of chloride ions. In contrast to the multiple product distribution on Cu electrode, a high CO2-to-CO selectivity up to ∼82% at −1.1 V versus RHE has been achieved on the Sbmodified Cu electrode. By combining in situ ATR-SEIRAS measurement and DFT calculations, it is revealed that the Sb and Cu bimetallic interface plays a vital role in determining the high CO selectivity by tuning the electronic structures of Cu and Sb and thus weakening the *CO binding strength on exposed Cu sites. We believe that these findings will shed light on the rational design of highly selective CO2 reduction catalysts as well as the interfacial structure engineering.
